summary: This work develops pulse-level control strategies to suppress residual XY coupling crosstalk in superconducting qubit processors during single-qubit operations and idle periods. Two methods are proposed: frequency modulation (FM) applying sinusoidal Z-drives and dynamical decoupling (DD) applying periodic Z-pulses, both engineered to average out the exchange interaction through phase accumulation.
motivation: As superconducting processors scale to larger qubit counts with dense connectivity, frequency crowding prevents maintaining large detunings between neighbors, causing XY crosstalk to emerge as a dominant coherent error source during single-qubit operations despite being suppressed by detuning in sparse architectures.
method: The approach exploits the oscillatory dependence of the XY term $H_{XY} = J(\sigma_1^+ \sigma_2^- e^{i\Delta t} + \text{h.c.})$ on detuning $\Delta$. At matched gate times $T_M = 2m\pi/|\Delta|$ the first-order error vanishes. FM with amplitude $\gamma$ and modulation cycles $N$ further suppresses second-order errors by modulating the instantaneous detuning, while DD Z-4 uses four equally-spaced $\pi$ pulses over $T_M$ to invert and average the crosstalk in alternating segments.
result: Numerical simulations with $\Delta/2\pi = 50$ MHz and $J/2\pi = 5$ MHz show FM reduces idle-gate infidelity by $>4$ orders of magnitude (reaching $\sim 6$ orders with $N=8$), and X-gate infidelity by $>2$ orders; DD Z-4 achieves $\sim 1$ order reduction for idle gates and $\sim 0.37$ orders for X-gates. Both methods maintain suppression over 20+ consecutive operations and scale to a five-qubit central-neighbor configuration with comparable relative performance despite higher absolute infidelities from multiple coupling paths.
